newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia non-ferrous metals sector seeks state help.
newsitem.headline: Serbia non-ferrous metals sector seeks state help.

text.p: Serbia's non-ferrous metals companies urged the government on Monday to give them more protection and said total liberalisation of trade would only harm a branch that was the single biggest exporter in 1997.

"This is a sector of strategic interest for the state and the government must do more to help these firms get back on their feet," a representative of the Sevojno copper rolling mill told a meeting of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce non-ferrous metals committee.

The sector, which includes production of non-ferrous ores and metals and non-ferrous metals processing, exported $400-$500 million per year before the break-up of the former federation and the imposition of war-related U.N. sanctions on Yugoslavia in 1992.

"This branch could already be exporting $200 to $300 million per year, but the main obstacle remains working capital and credits to finance export-oriented production," said an official of the Jagodina cable factory Fabrika Kablova.

According to the Federal Statistics Office, in the January-May 1997 period Yugoslavia exported $999,000 worth of non-ferrous ores, $97.786 million of non-ferrous metals and $21.754 million of processed non-ferrous metals.
With exports of the three branches accounting for $120.5 million of total Yugoslav exports of $862 million in the first five months this year, it deserves more attention, industry sources said.

According to official statistics, in January 1997 Yugoslavia produced 9,718 tonnes of electrolytic copper, 1,550 tonnes of refined lead, 2,170 tonnes of zinc, 5,419 tonnes of aluminium and 4,936 kilograms of refined silver.
In the same month, copper ore output stood at 1.467 million tonnes and lead-zinc ore 58,000 tonnes.
